statement: Scientific results and evidence are strengthened when they can be independently replicated and confirmed by several separate researchers.
Researchers should properly document and share the data and processes tied to their analyses so the broader community can save time reproducing or building on the published results.
A significant proportion of scientific studies cannot be reproduced, which causes academics and society to lose trust in scientific results.
Publishing negative results helps others avoid wasting time repeating analyses that will not return the expected findings.
Reproducibility in data research is defined as the data and code being available to fully rerun the analysis.
A project should state which definition of reproducibility it uses, because several competing definitions are in circulation and readers otherwise misunderstand each other.
condition: several definitions of reproducibility are in use

statement: Host your own BinderHub instead of the public service when you need capabilities beyond its computational limits, such as authentication, more compute per user, bespoke library stacks, access to private repositories, persistent storage, or restricted sharing.
condition: needs exceed the public BinderHub's computational limits

statement: repo2docker automatically builds a Docker image from a code repository given a configuration file, bundling the code, data, and preinstalled software needed to run it.
Binder aids reproducibility because it requires the code to be version controlled and the computational environment to be documented before it can run.
Each change to a Binder code repository forces a new build, which acts as a proxy for continuous integration because the instance breaks if the configuration file is not kept up to date.
Keep in version control all of the code required to produce a manuscript from scratch.

Making all code available in a self-contained repository is not by itself sufficient for reproducibility, because installing the same versions of tools such as LaTeX, Jupyter, and R can still be difficult for less experienced users.
Combine repo2docker with a BinderHub hosting service to give readers an interactive copy of a repository with all required software preinstalled at exactly the right versions.
Use version-stable Binder links pinned to a git tag so that shared links stay valid and point to the same repository state even after later corrections.
condition: sharing a link to a specific repository state

statement: Use a workflow manager such as Snakemake to define every step required to reproduce an entire manuscript from scratch.

Pre-build the computational container and reuse it in continuous integration rather than rebuilding it every run, because the environment changes far less often than the repository contents and this saves computing time.
Use continuous integration to check pull-request contributions for technical integrity and to keep the latest required container available for direct download.
Link a GitHub repository to Zenodo to ensure long-term archiving and citability through a DOI.
GitHub Actions workflow files are written in YAML and must be stored in the .github/workflows directory of the repository.
A GitHub Actions workflow's on field declares the events that trigger it, such as a push or pull_request on a given branch.
By default, when a step in a GitHub Actions job fails, the subsequent steps of that job are skipped.
Each run keyword in a GitHub Actions step starts a new process and shell, while multiple lines under one run command execute in the same shell.
Use the GitHub-provided actions/checkout action so a workflow can access the contents of the repository it runs against.
GitHub Actions is an event-driven task-automation system integrated with GitHub that triggers a workflow in response to repository events such as a pull request or issue being created.
A GitHub Actions workflow is a unit of automation composed of one or more jobs, and each job is composed of sequential steps.
In GitHub Actions, jobs run in parallel by default while the steps within a job run sequentially by default.

Use the continuous-integration configuration of well-maintained open-source projects as a starting template, because their licence usually permits copying the parts relevant to your case and their setups already work.
condition: the source project's licence permits copying its configuration

statement: Continuous integration is the practice of integrating individual contributors' changes into a shared main version frequently, usually multiple times per day, so conflicts and bugs are found and fixed early while the effort to fix them is small.

Team members should integrate their work frequently, ideally at least daily, rather than working in isolation and merging large changes infrequently, because infrequent integration makes merges very difficult when contributors have made contradictory changes.
Each integration should be verified by an automated build that usually includes tests, so integration errors are detected as quickly as possible.
It is easier to fix a bug in code you wrote a few minutes ago than in code you wrote yesterday, last week, or last month, which is why early detection matters.

Integrating code frequently by itself gives no guarantee about the quality of the new code, so an automated build-and-test run after each merge is the necessary second aspect of continuous integration.
Encourage project members to make and commit small changes, because small changes minimise the probability and impact of problems arising during integration.

Use trunk-based development, doing work in the main branch or merging back frequently and keeping any feature branches short-lived and small, so conflicts are surfaced while their scope is still small.
Keep the build and test phases fast and treat any increase in build time as a major problem, because every commit kicks off a build so the cost is compounded.
Run independent sections of the test suite in parallel to move the build through the pipeline faster.
condition: the test sections are independent and parallelisable

statement: Weight a test suite toward fast, low-maintenance unit tests, include a fair number of integration tests, and back off on the more complex and breakage-prone system or acceptance tests.

When software is too computationally expensive to test fully in continuous integration, use tiered testing with a broad common subgroup run every time plus additional targeted subgroups selected by what changed, to balance test coverage against a usable development process.
condition: building or running the software requires significant compute resource

statement: Check for dependency updates regularly, because it avoids bugs caused by code depending on deprecated functionality.
Build the project once at the start of the pipeline and reuse that exact stored artefact in every later phase, so different build tools cannot introduce inconsistencies between phases.
A continuous-integration workflow should install the project's required dependencies and then run its test suite, returning the results on each new pushed commit.
When continuous integration reports that a commit causes a test to fail, find and fix the problem as soon as possible.
Document the source code of software regardless of how time-consuming it is, so others can understand why the software exists, how it was built, and how to use or reuse it.
Use the Diataxis framework to organise extended software documentation into four distinct types: tutorials, how-to guides, explanations, and reference guides.

Tutorials teach use of the software step by step, how-to guides give the steps to solve a particular problem, explanations provide context and understanding, and reference guides describe functions, inputs, outputs, and when they can or cannot be used.
Comment only what is necessary in code and explain why something was done rather than aiming to comment every single line.
Some documentation is better than no documentation.
Not every project needs extensive documentation; decide the level of documentation from the audience and the code's complexity, since sometimes a basic README and a few code comments are sufficient.
exception: the audience and complexity are small enough that a README and a few comments suffice

statement: Provide a README that introduces and explains the project, giving the information commonly needed to understand what the project is about.
Provide contributing guidelines describing how people can contribute to the software, which are especially important in open-source projects.
Maintain a roadmap of current and future development plans so users know when to expect new or removed features and developers can avoid duplicating effort.
Keep a changelog, a plain-text file recording the notable changes made between versions of the software.
Include a licence for the software so users know under what legal conditions they are allowed to use it.
Define a code of conduct when collaboration is an important aspect of the project, to create and maintain an environment that promotes participation and mutual respect among contributors.
condition: collaboration is an important aspect of the project

statement: Provide a CITATION.cff file containing citation metadata so people know how to cite your software.
Name files so they are readable by both humans and machines: avoid wildcard characters, use underscores to delimit information and dashes to join words, and avoid vague labels such as FINAL.
Date files in ISO long format YYYY-MM-DD followed by the file name and version number, so that files automatically sort into chronological order.
Version software using a Major.Minor.Patch scheme rather than ad-hoc labels like _FINAL, so the version is unambiguous and you avoid final-final naming.
Choose a single variable-naming convention and use it consistently throughout your code, because switching between different formats makes code difficult to read.
Store the result of a transformation in a new, descriptively named variable rather than reusing the original variable name, so the transformations that have been applied remain visible.
Write clear, well-commented, readable, and reusable code, because readability benefits you and everyone else who later reads or reuses it, whatever the scale of the project.
Keep code lines to roughly 79 to 80 characters so they fit on a screen; a line longer than this can be a sign that a function is too complex and should be broken up.
Keep comments clear and concise so they record the decisions you made and what functions and variables do, letting others follow your thought process; use inline comments sparingly.
Use consistent indentation, such as two spaces rather than a mixture of tabs and spaces, and agree a common style when collaborating.
Describe your coding style in a readme file so that collaborators or contributors can follow your lead.
In Markdown source, start a new line after every sentence (a semantic line break), which makes the raw text easier to read, review, and diff without changing the rendered output.
condition: working in Markdown or similar markup source

statement: Noticing that something is wrong is the first step to fixing it, so a program needs built-in checks so that problems are not missed.
A silent failure occurs when an assumption the program relies on is wrong for a specific case but the program carries on regardless, producing wrong results that are hard to detect.
Make the assumptions in your code explicit, focusing especially on assumptions about the data and files a user puts into your workflow.
Assert or verify your assumptions with checks such as an if/else block so the program can alert a user when an important condition is not met.
When an assumption or condition is not met, decide deliberately for each case whether to redirect the program, report to the user, or abort execution.
A warning indicates a potential problem without stopping the program, whereas an error is thrown when the program needs to halt.
Raise your own warnings or errors rather than relying only on built-in ones, because doing so lets you control the quality of the message and give the user instructions on how to fix the problem.

Write informative, actionable error messages that clearly pinpoint the problem, point the user to next steps, use jargon appropriately for the audience, and are honest about what they do and do not know.
A program should fail informatively rather than failing silently or with a cryptic message.
Use exception handling (a try/except or try/catch block) to catch an expected error and change the program's course instead of stopping.
Use tests to complement robustness checks: pass strange data to your workflow to confirm it redirects, reports, or aborts as expected, and confirm you receive the expected error messages.
Use automatic code-formatting tools to enforce a consistent style, which raises code quality and matters most when collaborating in a team where others must read your code.
Adopt a consistent indentation standard such as 2-space or 4-space indentation, which is highly recommended because it increases the chance of finding bugs.
Use a language-independent tool such as EditorConfig to keep whitespace styles consistent across multiple people and editors working on the same project.
Linters analyse code to find potential errors, style violations, and other issues without running the code, and are best used early and often in a project.
Static code analysis examines code to detect vulnerabilities, quality issues, and security weaknesses before the code is executed or deployed, and can also help maintain a consistent coding style.
Use a code-quality service that integrates with your GitHub or GitLab repository, because it can detect and communicate quality issues directly in pull requests.
Consistently using one coding style throughout code makes it easier to read and understand, which reduces the risk of mistakes and makes it easier to work together on software.
Choose a coding-style framework suited to your purpose and remain consistent with it, rather than being consistently inconsistent.
Make sure that you or somebody else can reuse your code to do the same exact thing you did and obtain the same results.
Store code publicly, share it with collaborators, and give it a unique persistent identifier so that everyone can find and access it.
Document the temporal evolution of code with version control so that a specific version from the past can be retrieved.

Script the computational environment so it can be recreated on demand and run the sequence of operations with a pipeline script, so that no human is needed to replicate the work; scripting the steps also serves as documentation.
Attach a license to your code, prefer a permissive license that allows reuse, and choose one compatible with the licenses of the libraries and packages your software depends on.
Make your code citable by specifying how you want to be cited when people reuse it.
If the software depends on any data, make that data available alongside the code.
condition: the software depends on data

statement: Remove hardcoded specifics such as data details, analysis parameters, and machine-specific file paths, make the code modular, and pass file paths as command-line arguments to produce a more portable and reusable script.
Make modules pure: given the same input a pure function always returns the same value.
Test that the modules you write accept different types of input data or parameters, which also documents which inputs are allowed and how the code should not be used.
Turn reusable modules into a package or toolbox to separate the specifics of your project from the parts that can be reused in other projects or by other people.

Document the environment the code lived in, including the operator's steps, hardware, operating system, libraries, and dependencies, because the environment is a fragile snapshot in time that silently accompanies the code.

It often pays more to write code so other humans, including your future self, can read it; a cryptic one-liner with obscure variable names is no faster or more efficient than splitting it into multiple readable steps.
Write comments before writing the actual code, so that someone could read only the comments and get a full picture of what the code does.

Useful documentation is required at every level of reuse, with more documentation needed for higher levels: usage, options, and examples for repeatable reuse, and installation instructions covering hardware, tested operating system, and software requirements for portable reuse.
A package (also called a library or module) is a basic unit of reproducible and often efficient code that creates or extends the functionality of a programming language.

When writing a package for others to use, ensure the code works reliably on systems other than your own by using unit and integration testing, version control, documentation, accessible hosting, and continuous-integration pipelines.
Consider submitting a package to a central resource such as CRAN, PyPI, or npm and writing a publication, so the package can be peer-reviewed and users gain more confidence that it is robust.
Use a package template or scaffolding tool to create the underlying package structure, including documentation locations, comment conventions, and built-in linting, rather than starting from scratch.
Make your code reusable regardless of project size, following the reuse recommendations that suit your type of software and skipping the ones that are not relevant.
Different software has different reuse requirements: a small script may need only sufficient documentation, while a mission-critical software library may require thorough testing.
Follow the FAIR Principles for Research Software (FAIR4RS) as a more elaborate approach to making research software reusable.
Freire and Chirigati define five levels of reproducibility according to what can be modified: repeatable, re-runnable, portable, extendable, and modifiable.
A research compendium is a collection of all the digital parts of a research project, including data, code, texts, and metadata, organised so that reproducing all results is straightforward.

Publish your research paper together with a research compendium so others can access your inputs, test your analysis, and, if it is executable, rerun it to assess the output, which builds trust in your research and gives you more visibility.
Construct a research compendium on three principles: organise files in a conventional folder structure, clearly separate data, methods, and output, and specify the computational environment.

Give any research compendium a landing-page README, and for an executable compendium describe the environment in a Dockerfile and the file dependencies and build steps in a Makefile, plus include a LICENSE and a CITATION file.

Separate the files in a compendium into read-only (raw data and metadata), human-generated (code, paper, documentation), and project-generated (clean data, figures, other output), recognising that a file's category can change over the project life cycle.
A version-control repository can itself be a research compendium: a Makefile makes it executable and a reproducible environment makes it reproducible.

When creating a research compendium, first identify the components of your project and build the folder structure accordingly, using file and folder names that make it easy for others to understand their contents.
Start a research project early with the mindset that the final output is a research compendium rather than just a research paper.
Publish a research compendium on a versioning platform such as GitHub or GitLab, on a research archive such as Zenodo or the OSF, or as supplementary material to a paper.
Keep a compendium as clean and easy to use as possible, and optionally have a peer check that it works correctly before you publish it.

Add a dedicated license file to the repository, choose a license suitable for the content (using multiple licenses for mixed content, for example CC-BY for text and MIT for software), and note the license in the README.

Combining multiple external components can impose multiple constraints on the combined work's license, and if those constraints conflict the licenses are incompatible and the result cannot be legally distributed.

Check that the licenses of components you combine are compatible before distributing the combined work, because incompatible licenses can make distributing, or even creating, the combined work illegal.

Copyleft licenses require modified versions to be distributed under the same license and, if a binary is distributed, that the source code be included, whereas permissive licenses grant the largest set of permissions to users.

Strong copyleft requires the whole combined work to be licensed under the component's license, while weak copyleft allows the combined work under any license as long as the copyleft component's source stays available under its original license.
The GNU GPL is incompatible with proprietary licenses because it requires the combined work to be licensed under the GPL with no additional restrictions allowed.

When distributing a combined work, answer three questions: which separate works exist and what is derived from what; whether the derivative works can be distributed and their licenses are compatible; and how the works should be licensed.
When redistributing a third-party component you do not own, distribute it under the license its authors granted; you cannot add or remove permissions on code whose copyright you do not hold.
Choose your own code's license so it is compatible with at least one license under which your dependencies can be distributed, so that others can assemble and distribute combined works.

The GPL permits unlimited private modification as long as the modified software is not distributed, while under the AGPL letting users interact with the software over a network counts as distribution and obliges you to provide the source code.
Exchanging materials with a different legal entity, such as a collaborator outside your organisation, counts as distribution for licensing purposes.
To avoid forming a single combined work from incompatible licenses, split the system into independent programs that run in separate processes and communicate over well-documented, generic interfaces.
exception: how separate the programs must be to not count as a single work is legally unclear

statement: Avoid combining strong-copyleft dependencies with proprietary components in a single project you intend to distribute, and if it is unavoidable tread carefully because it carries legal risk.

A data license governs what others can do with data you make accessible and varies on attribution to the owner, permission to redistribute or modify, and whether derivatives must carry the same license.
The data license you choose directly affects how accessible your data is to others.
Creative Commons licenses, although not tailored for data, can be used as data licenses in some cases, such as CC0 for public-domain data or the commonly used CC-BY license.
condition: the data-use case fits the Creative Commons terms

statement: CC0 dedicates work to the public domain by relinquishing all copyright and the right to attribution, so recognition as the creator then relies on citation norms in academic communities.
Open Data Commons provides three licenses designed specifically for data, each accompanied by a human-readable summary of its legal effect.
The Open Data Commons PDDL waives all rights to the data, analogous to CC0, and comes with recommended but non-mandatory community norms that guide fair, open sharing of data.
The ODC-BY license protects the data owner's attribution rights, requiring any use or distribution of the database to include information on the license used with the original.

The ODbL adds share-alike, requiring public uses of the data to carry the same license, and requires that any version redistributed in a closed format also be made available in a version free of such closure measures.

Open Data Commons licenses were made specifically for data and typically cover only database rights, whereas Creative Commons licenses are general-purpose and also cover copyright and neighbouring rights.

License documentation and creative outputs with an appropriate license so users know how the materials can be used, copied, or shared, applying different licenses to different artefacts where needed, such as a Creative Commons license for documentation and MIT for code.

Creative Commons offers six license types plus a public-domain dedication tool, ranging from most to least permissive and varying on whether they require attribution, allow commercial use, allow modification, and allow changing the license.
Decide which license fits your work by thinking about why you want to share it and how you hope others will use it.

A Creative Commons share-alike (SA) term forbids changing the license when redistributing, a no-derivatives (ND) term forbids modifying or adapting the work, and a non-commercial (NC) term forbids commercial use.
Software you are not allowed to copy or modify, or that carries usage restrictions such as research-use-only or non-commercial-use-only, is proprietary rather than free or libre.
Permissively licensed content can generally be used by anyone for any purpose and can be modified and redistributed under a different license, including as part of a closed or for-profit project.

Copyleft content, whether modified or unmodified, must be distributed under the same or a compatible license that retains the copyleft obligation, so modifications of copyleft content must also be copyleft.

The Free Software Foundation defines four fundamental software freedoms: to run the program for any purpose, to study and change it (requiring source access), to redistribute copies, and to distribute modified versions (requiring source access).

The term free or libre software emphasises liberty (free as in speech, not as in beer) and is associated with copyleft, while open source emphasises the freedom to study and modify and is associated with permissive licenses.
Open source software is free to use, but building and maintaining it requires extensive labour and resources that are not free and should not be trivialised.
Being a good open source citizen means playing by the license rules and, when you can, contributing your fixes and improvements to upstream projects rather than only freeloading off of them.

Contributing your changes upstream is often the simplest way to redistribute them and gains you the upstream maintainers' help keeping your code working, sparing you from maintaining your own fork, while everyone benefits from the shared improvements.
Copyleft licenses do not prohibit commercial use; many companies build copyleft projects and generate revenue through support services instead of selling licenses.

Usage-restricting licenses such as Ethical Source and Responsible AI licenses curtail freedom 0 by prohibiting certain uses, so by the classical FSF and OSI definitions they are not free or open source licenses, and their adoption has so far been relatively limited.
Even an attribution requirement can in some cases count as a usage restriction, and for academic works attribution requirements can reinforce the citation convention with the force of copyright law.

Choosing open infrastructure is important for including people who adhere strongly to the free-software ethos, because a small minority will not participate if doing so requires them to use non-free software.

Compliance with conventional free-software licenses is relatively easy to demonstrate by sharing the code, whereas compliance with ethical-source licenses can be considerably more complex and expensive to demonstrate and exposes a greater attack surface for bad-faith legal action.

Technical enforcement measures (DRM) are often brittle, invasive because they must run at the highest privilege that can then be abused, and ultimately bypassable, so anti-circumvention laws mainly burden law-abiding users while the intended targets circumvent them anyway.

Find approved open-source licenses from curated lists: the Open Source Initiative's approved-license list, the Free Software Foundation's list of GPL-compatible licenses and recommendations, and the guided tool at choosealicense.com.

Creative Commons licenses contain no specific terms about distributing source code, but can be combined with software licenses across the parts of an ML/AI system, applying CC to training data and weights and software licenses to the code used in training or deployment.

Copyleft license terms have been successfully defended in court, obliging abusers to release their code, but such violations are hard to discover because copyleft use is not obvious from a black-box proprietary end product.

The copyright holder of a copyleft project can still re-license or dual-license it, but in a community-developed project this requires the consent of every contributor, which is why some projects use Contributor License Agreements to assign or license contributors' copyright.
Source-available or shared-source projects publish their code but do not license its reuse, modification, or redistribution, so they are not open source.

Copyright protects only creative elements while functional items need a patent, and copyright and patent are mutually exclusive for a given thing, which complicates licensing hardware that mixes creative and functional elements.
For an open hardware project, plan to license the four OSHWA-certification elements separately as relevant: the hardware, the software, the documentation, and the branding.

Use a hardware-native license such as the CERN OHL, available in strongly reciprocal (S), weakly reciprocal (W), and permissive (P) variants, for the hardware design, because these licenses address the peculiarities of licensing open hardware.

License the software part of open hardware (including firmware, which is not counted as part of the hardware) with an OSI-approved license, and license the documentation with a CC license, using CC-BY for permissive and CC-BY-SA for copyleft.
For a project to be considered open source, no restriction on field of use or on commercial use may be placed on it.

Open hardware licenses are recent and largely untested in court and rest on copyright law that transfers poorly to hardware, so their protections are unproven and are best thought of as guiding tools for good actors, not ways to punish bad actors.

Anyone producing creative works governed by IP law, including documentation, software, datasets, and graphics, needs a basic understanding of it, and different project types may need different licensing choices from the outset to match their goals.

Copyright, patents, and trademarks all extend property rights to intangible goods so that others' use can be prevented or licensed, creating a limited grant of monopoly meant to incentivise creation and improvement.

Copyright, licenses, and patents are legal concepts subject to laws that differ between countries and change over time, so guidance based on one legal tradition may not apply in another, and you should consult a legal expert for actual legal advice.

By default an author retains all rights to a work made public under copyright, whereas a patent must be registered before the content is publicly disclosed, so you must patent something before sharing it publicly.

Some licenses, such as section 3 of the Apache 2.0 license, grant permission to use the authors' applicable patents so those patents do not impede use of the open software, but this cannot protect against patents held by third parties.

Trademarks primarily serve consumer protection by preventing bad actors from impersonating recognisable brands, must be registered (which can be done after public use), apply within a specific sector, and can matter when a project is renamed or forked.

Consider registering a trademark for an open source project, because its work can easily be cloned, modified, and redistributed with ill intent such as added malware, and trademark enforcement can in some cases help prevent or deter this.

By default, making a work public retains your copyright, so anyone reusing it must license the right from you or risk an infringement lawsuit, subject to fair-use or fair-dealing exceptions that are decided case by case.

US fair use is decided case by case on four factors: the purpose and character of the use (commercial versus nonprofit-educational), the nature of the work, the amount and substantiality of the portion used, and the effect on the potential market for the work.

Apply a pre-made off-the-shelf license tailored to your type of work, whether software, images or prose, hardware and designs, or ML models, rather than negotiating individual arrangements, because which license you choose shapes how others may reuse the work.
An ML or AI model comprises several separately licensable parts, including training data, code, and model weights, each of which may be licensed differently.

It is an open legal question whether ML model weights are copyrightable, because copyright excludes ideas, procedures, and algorithms and requires human creative authorship, so their status must be settled by courts or legislation.

Use a Responsible AI License to place use-based restrictions on an ML model when you want to release it openly for research or industry but restrict specific uses you are not comfortable with, choosing a research-only non-commercial variant or an open variant that permits commercial downstream distribution as appropriate.

An ML model license governs the use and redistribution of the model or algorithm and any derivatives, separately from the other components of an AI system such as data, source code, and applications, which may carry their own licenses.
The growing list of ML-specific licenses reflects the understanding that the ML model is distinct from its source code and therefore needs new licensing options.

Many versions of a model may exist, whether a model family or reimplementations in different frameworks, each potentially with its own license, and some developers now require downstream derived models to keep at least the same use restrictions as the original.

Standard open-source licenses do not take into account the technical nature and capabilities of an ML model as a distinct artefact, so they are ill-adapted to enabling more responsible use of ML models.

Responsible AI Licenses (RAIL), which emerged in 2019, add use-restriction clauses to mitigate potential harms from AI artefacts and give the licensor the capacity to enforce against an identified misuse of the model.
RAIL license modifiers denote which component the use restrictions apply to: D for the training data, A for the application or service, M for the model, and S for the source code.

A RAIL-M license restricts using the model for harmful or illegal purposes, such as breaking the law, harming minors, generating disinformation or non-consensual impersonation, distributing undisclosed machine-generated content, discriminating against protected groups, or making automated decisions that adversely affect an individual's legal rights.

An OpenRAIL license is both open, granting royalty-free access and flexible downstream use and redistribution of the artefact and its derivatives, and responsible, embedding a set of use restrictions for identified critical scenarios such as illegal, discriminatory, or misinformation content.

Every RAIL or OpenRAIL license requires that its set of use restrictions also be included in any subsequent redistribution or derivative version of the model, to dissuade users of derivatives from misuse.

There is currently no effective copyleft equivalent among OpenRAIL licenses: they require only that the use restrictions be retained in derived works, not that the contained software or model weights be similarly licensed.

RAIL and OpenRAIL licenses should not impose use restrictions so excessive that they hinder incremental innovation, and a licensor may at their discretion make an exception and open some restrictions when a licensee shows the model was modified to remove the specific concern.

A model's chosen license reflects the licensor's business, research, or ethics-informed values and signals to users how the model should be used, so licensing choices differ across models from permissive (for example MIT) to research-only or Open and Responsible AI licenses.

A license is a legal agreement between the creator or owner of a resource and its users that defines the scope of what users can and cannot do with the work, protecting the creator's rights while granting users limited rights.

General licensing guidance written by engineers and scientists is a heavily simplified overview and is not legal advice, so do not base important decisions on it alone and consult a librarian and a legal expert for advice on your case.

Make the license clearly visible by placing a plain-text LICENSE file in the project's top-level directory so hosts like GitHub or GitLab pick it up, and prefer a license that has a standardised SPDX short name so hosts can display it.

Include license information as standard strings at the top of each text file, especially when a project contains material licensed in multiple different ways, and use tools such as REUSE to automate this.
condition: the project mixes multiple licenses or is reused elsewhere

statement: A build system relies on a directed acyclic graph (DAG): edges have a direction that constrains traversal, and the graph contains no cycles, so a target cannot depend on another that depends back on it.
Prefer GNU Make over the BSD version of Make, because some Makefile features may not work as expected under BSD Make.
When applying multiple similar scripts to the same data, use a canned recipe (a parameterised rule template) so you avoid writing an almost-identical Make rule for each script.
condition: many Make rules differ only in the script name

statement: Run Make with parallel jobs, for example make -j 4, to build independent targets concurrently and speed up the build.

CSV files are often messy and use uncommon dialects such as strange delimiters and uncommon quote or escape characters, so standard CSV readers may load them incorrectly and data scientists waste time on data-wrangling.
When using Make for reproducibility, start small and start early, growing the Makefile iteratively from running the core analysis to generating the figures, tables, and manuscript.
Provide a data-collection target, such as make data, that downloads public source data via a script so that anyone can obtain the inputs needed to reproduce the work.
condition: the data comes from public sources

statement: Include grouping PHONY targets, such as make figures, that depend on all outputs of a given type so a whole class of results can be recreated with a single command.
Generate result tables as LaTeX files so they can be directly included in the LaTeX source of the manuscript.
Guard cleaning rules that delete outputs which take a while to recreate behind a confirmation target that asks the user to confirm before proceeding.
condition: the outputs being removed are slow to regenerate

statement: Keeping the code, results, and manuscript in a single Make-built repository is especially useful for collaboration because only one repository needs to be shared.

Debug a Makefile by printing variable values with the info function, halting execution at a point with the error function, tracing which rules Make tries with make -d, and dry-running without executing with make -n (combined as make -dn).
Make rebuilds an output file when any of its prerequisites change, which is a core reason Make exists: to update outputs when their source files change.
Makefile recipes must be indented with tabs; Makefiles do not accept indentation with spaces.

Make executes each recipe line independently in a separate subshell, so a directory change on one line has no effect on the next and a failure on one line does not stop the following lines, which is why dependent commands must be combined into a single recipe line.
Make runs the first target when none is given, so by convention the first target is named all and lists the desired outputs as its prerequisites.
Provide a clean target to remove outputs and start fresh, using the -f flag to rm so it does not complain when a file is already absent.
Declare targets that do not create an output file, such as all, clean, and test, as .PHONY so they always run and are not shadowed by a file or directory of the same name.
Use automatic variables such as $< for the first prerequisite and $@ for the target, together with pattern rules using the % wildcard, to collapse near-identical rules and avoid repeating yourself.
Use Make functions such as wildcard, filter-out, and patsubst to build target lists from the files in an input directory when pattern rules alone are insufficient.
A Makefile convention is to name variables in all capitals and define them at the top of the file.
Develop your directory structure and your Makefile hand in hand, since a cleaner directory layout can let simpler pattern rules suffice.
Avoid recursive, nested Makefiles, because Make then cannot see the entire dependency graph, which leads to problems.

Inject computed numerical results into a manuscript automatically, either by writing them out as a LaTeX table file included with input, or by having the analysis script emit LaTeX variable definitions via newcommand that the manuscript then substitutes in.
Automatically inserting computed results into the manuscript prevents mistakes from manually copying results into tables and makes the research more accessible and reproducible.

Snakemake is a Python3-based alternative to Make that supports multiple wildcards in filenames, allows Python code in rules, and can run workflows on workstations, clusters, grids, and the cloud without modification.

A data-science project can be seen as a tree of dependencies where the report depends on figures and tables that depend on the data and analysis scripts, and Make builds outputs from those dependencies through rules, so combining the two ideas creates a reproducible project.

Makefiles are human-readable and machine-readable text that both document the build for a person and are executed by a computer, are easy to share and version-control, and reduce cognitive load because the conventional all and clean targets let someone run the project without lengthy instructions.

A clever Makefile lets you share a complete analysis of code, data, and workflow so collaborators or readers can recompute your results, which increases trust in the output, makes the research more accessible, and eases collaboration.

Open Access means free availability of full texts on the public internet to read, download, copy, distribute, print, search, or link, with copyright's only role being to give authors control over the integrity of their work and the right to be acknowledged and cited.

A preprint is a scientific manuscript that authors upload to a public server before peer review, which lets researchers share results quickly and get feedback on the manuscript before submitting it to a journal.

Most preprint servers automatically assign a DOI when you deposit a manuscript, making the work citable even before peer review, and the preprint DOI is a separate, independent record from any future journal-publication DOI.

There are three main routes to Open Access: posting preprints and self-archiving (both called green or gratis Open Access), and Gold Open Access where an article-processing charge makes the published version openly and freely available under a license whose copyright the author retains.

Follow Think.Check.Submit guidelines to avoid predatory journals that trick authors into paying an article-processing charge without providing genuine editorial processes to check article quality and legitimacy.

Hybrid journals, which are subscription journals offering a per-article charge to make content open, are criticised as double-dipping because publishers are paid by authors to open content while also selling the subscription to universities.

Before self-archiving, check the journal's copyright policy for which version may be deposited (submitted preprint, accepted postprint, or published version of record) and after what embargo period, which can range from zero to 60 months.
Research is useless if it is not shared, and sharing openly helps researchers work more effectively, avoids duplication of effort, and makes results more likely to be checked and reproduced.
Publishing openly benefits the author, because the work is likely to reach a larger audience with broader societal impact and openly published papers are more likely to have a citation advantage.

To open your data, put it in a simple standard machine- and human-readable format, provide metadata describing what it is, how it was collected, and its strengths and weaknesses, host it in a discoverable trusted repository, and assign it a persistent identifier such as a DOI.

To open your software, put the code in a freely accessible repository, include a license granting rights to use, copy, and modify it, include a README covering what it is and how to install, use, and test it, and add contribution guidelines if you want collaborators.
To open your hardware, use open hardware where practical, make detailed documentation and designs openly available, include a license granting rights to use, copy, and modify, and include a README.

Only a very small proportion of original research data is published; in practice data are stored in private files rather than secure institutional repositories and are effectively lost to the public and often even to the researcher who generated them.
It is generally difficult or impossible to reproduce a study without the original data, and the data cannot be reused or built upon by other researchers if they cannot obtain access to it.
Open data is freely available on the internet, permitting any user to download, copy, analyse, reprocess, and reuse it for any purpose with minimal financial, legal, and technical barriers.

Adopt an open-by-default stance for data, presuming publication for all, and keep data only as closed as necessary, making the justification clear when access must be restricted, for example for security reasons.

Surveyed researchers name the main barriers to data sharing as the difficulty of organising data presentably (46%), uncertainty about copyright and licensing (37%), and not knowing which repository to use for different data types (33%).

For anonymised research data to be shareable for reuse, the consent forms must cover sharing the data with other researchers, and participant information sheets should state how the data will be stored, preserved, used long-term, and kept confidential.
condition: the data concerns human research participants

statement: Some data legitimately cannot be made fully open for legal, ethical, privacy, national-security, or commercial-sensitivity reasons, in which case it may only be possible to share partial or obscured datasets.
exception: legal, ethical, privacy, security, or commercial-sensitivity constraints apply

statement: Open source hardware refers to the design specifications of a physical object licensed so that the specifications and the object can be studied, modified, created, and distributed by anyone, where hardware means any tangible object such as machines, electronic devices, biomaterials, or textiles.

Like open source software, the source of open hardware is available for anyone to modify or enhance, but unlike plain-text code it consists of schematics, blueprints, logic and CAD designs, and files that mix text, binary, and software.

Open hardware projects should share both raw and derived source files, for example a print-ready .stl together with the modifiable 3D-object format, because the raw files are needed to enable modification even if they require proprietary software and specific skills.
Be open from the very beginning of an open hardware project, starting at the description-of-needs phase, rather than only sharing the design once you reach the demonstrator stage.

An open hardware project emerges from a concrete need and moves through prototyping to a demonstrator, which solves the need but is not yet ready to replicate, and then to a market-ready product that is polished, documented, and ready for hardware producers.

When an open hardware need arises, scope the project and invest time looking for similar existing projects to join rather than starting a new one, because this can save time and hassle and may reveal collaborators and refine your ideas.
Early in an open hardware project, draw a roadmap and identify future users, contributors, and manufacturers with complementary skills, and decide on a license.

Open hardware gives an individual researcher flexibility and speed to customise designs without depending on vendors, a lower price than proprietary equipment, and control to keep systems running even if a supplier goes out of business.

Open hardware benefits science through quality (contributors offer novel solutions and catch errors), reproducibility (designs can be replicated and calibration controlled), inclusiveness (cheaper equipment enables science where resources are scarce), and sustainability (local repair extends lifespan and reduces waste).

Building and developing open hardware can require specific skills and significant time, so buying industrial hardware with the vendor's client support may be cheaper, especially without enough in-house technical support.
condition: you lack sufficient in-house technical support

statement: Share the hardware source with an appropriate license via an online platform, tailoring how much content to share to the hardware's complexity and community importance, since the more you share the more the community can benefit and give back.

Provide at minimum a license and a README that describes the hardware's identity and purpose for a general audience, explaining what the project is and what it is for before getting into technical details.

Write open hardware documentation with the audience in mind and provide a list of the skills required to build, maintain, or operate the hardware, because building from scratch, maintenance, and end-use each need a distinct skillset and documentation.
Take particular care with safety instructions in open hardware documentation, because makers are not always formally trained engineers and may not easily tell dangerous manipulations from safe ones.
Provide technical documents that serve as the hardware's source code, such as technical drawings, electronic schematics, CAD files, and assembly instructions needed to study and replicate the design.

Include a Bill of Materials listing part numbers, suppliers, costs, and descriptions, and make it easy to tell which item corresponds to which component using matching reference designators or a diagram.

Ideally design open hardware using free and open source software to maximise others' ability to view and edit it, and share the original design files in both their original and an accessible ready-to-view format.

Provide complete build-and-run documentation for open hardware: assembly instructions with annotated photos or 3D renderings, a list of required tools and settings, any code or firmware with its build process and dependencies, and instructions for operation, calibration, maintenance, repair, and disposal.
Build modular and extensible hardware with documented interfaces, which eases maintenance and repair and makes it possible to grow a developer community around the project.

Be honest with collaborators and yourself about what support they can expect, and state plainly when maintainers lack the time to write documentation or review contributions, to avoid generating false expectations.

Make an open hardware project discoverable by using a commonly used platform, adding descriptive metadata such as a short description, a license statement, and project context (for example an Open Know-How manifest), and preparing shareable media.

Make open hardware citable and archive a version through a platform that assigns a persistent identifier such as a DOI (for example Zenodo), so specific versions or releases remain available over the long term, which is necessary for reproducibility.

Without an open license others cannot legally use, copy, distribute, or modify a hardware project, and hardware licensing is more complex than for software because patent law rather than copyright sometimes applies and different parts may need different licenses.

Electronic Lab Notebooks store experimental procedures, protocols, plans, notes, and data digitally and offer advantages over paper notebooks: searchability within and across notebooks, secure redundant storage, remote access, and easy sharing among collaborators.

Open notebook research is the practice of making notebooks openly available online, often from the start of a project and in real time, which reduces duplication of work, fosters collaboration, and helps researchers avoid repeating dead ends already explored but left unpublished by others.

Keeping an open notebook increases the quality of scientific outputs by forcing researchers to be careful, thorough, and explicit, and increases the chance that errors are spotted quickly while fixes are still cheap.
Adopt the principle of making open what you can, practising any form of open notebook research even partially, rather than requiring complete open access before you share anything.

Open scholarship means being open to everyone without discrimination, so communities should deliberately foster welcoming, inclusive cultures and make reasonable accommodations, which can be as simple as choosing colourblind-safe colour schemes for graphs.
Citizen science is the involvement of the public in scientific research, which engages the broader world in science and gives researchers human resources that would not otherwise be accessible.

Patient and Public Involvement means patients and members of the public contribute at all stages of the research cycle, which is distinct from participation (contributing data) and engagement (dissemination), and means working with volunteers rather than doing work about them.

Consider Patient and Public Involvement very early in a project, ideally before grant applications or ethics submissions, so volunteers can help shape research questions, study design, applications, data collection and analysis, and dissemination.
condition: the research concerns health or social issues

statement: When software is open source, anybody can view, use, modify, and distribute its source code for any purpose, enforced through an open-source license, which lowers the barriers to adoption and lets ideas spread quickly.

Producing widely-used research software through a closed-source approach would likely be infeasible or require a budget of tens of millions of dollars, because such packages depend on unsolicited community contributions that open source enables.

Open source software benefits research by being reusable (letting researchers build on each other's work and focus on unsolved problems), checkable (the community reads and tests the code so bugs are found and results validated), and collaborative (enabling projects no single group could build).

Contributing to open source software benefits you by improving technical and people skills, building cleaner maintainable-code habits, and making your work publicly visible so employers can see your ability and how you work with others, which can advance your career and reputation.

Reuse the best existing open-source solution rather than reinventing wheels, since many common problems are already solved, which reduces duplication of effort and frees researchers to focus on yet-unsolved challenges.
You must include a license file stating that anyone has permission to use, copy, and modify your work; without this no one can legally use your work and it is not open source.
Assign your code a DOI to make it citeable, which helps ensure you get proper credit when people use or build upon your work.

Include a README covering the project name and what it is and its main features, installation instructions with prerequisites, how to run the code and its tests, links to related material, a list of authors and contributors with contact information, and acknowledgements.
Write up installation instructions the first time you do the installation yourself, because it saves hours of work later for you and for anyone else setting up the project.

If you intend for others to collaborate on your project, include contributing guidelines that explain how to file bugs, suggest features, and get in touch, and most likely a code of conduct, keeping both in the root directory and linking to them from the README.
condition: you want others to collaborate rather than just consume the code

statement: Adopt an emerging standard code of conduct such as the Contributor Covenant rather than writing your own, and be prepared to enforce it when necessary.

A typical open source project has distinct roles: author (creator), owner (administrative owner), maintainers (drive the vision and organisation), contributors (anyone who contributes back), and community members (users), so identifying them helps you orient to a new project.

When contributing to another open source project, first read its documentation and contributing guidelines, match the style and conventions of the main project, and break your changes into manageable, well-defined chunks so they are simpler to understand and review.

Test your contributed changes against an up-to-date version of the project, write specific tests for the changes and submit them, and update the relevant documentation rather than submitting code alone.

When submitting a contribution, clearly describe what changes you made, why you made them, and how they were implemented, for example in the pull request, so a maintainer can more easily decide whether to incorporate the work.

Contribute to the open source projects you already use and keep coming back to, acting on any instinct that something could be better, such as a typo, a broken link, a bug, or a missing piece of documentation, rather than ignoring it or asking someone else to fix it.

Contributing to open source does not require writing code; the non-code parts such as documentation, usage examples, reviewing others' submissions, answering questions, and triaging issues are often the most neglected and are valuable contributions.

When working with closed software, recognise there are usually good reasons for it such as legal, commercial, or security concerns, and that the same reproducibility practices, concepts, and tools still apply even though the details of contributing may differ.

Open research aims to make research more reproducible, transparent, reusable, collaborative, accountable, and accessible by making the primary outputs of publicly funded research, its publications and data, publicly accessible in digital format with no or minimal restriction.

To achieve openness, each element of the research process should be publicly available (not behind passwords or paywalls), reusable (licensed appropriately so users know any reuse limitations), and transparent (with metadata clearly stating how the output was produced and what it contains).

Open research comprises open data, open source software, open hardware, open access, and open notebooks, and open scholarship extends it further to open educational resources, equity/diversity/inclusion, and citizen science.

Sharing errors you find in your own work is heavily disincentivised, because putting code and data online is revealing and intimidating, even though no law governs the communication of reproducible research short of explicit fraud.

Publishing your code and data documentation motivates you to conduct analyses to a higher standard and lets others give feedback and learn, so research culture should move away from treating publishing nothing as safer than publishing something.

Publication bias rewards novel findings, so papers that fail to find significance or that reproduce already-published results are hard to publish, which disincentivises documenting, testing, and sharing code and data and likely causes much duplicated work.
A researcher who shares code and data may be held to a higher standard than one who shares nothing, because reviewers can then scrutinise the implementation and may demand additional changes.
Overcome the incentive-structure barriers to reproducibility by aligning career incentives so that doing what is best for science also benefits the individual researchers involved.

Big data and complex computational infrastructure make reproducibility hard: obtaining identical data across runs is difficult (especially with parallel computing and streamed data), software performance varies across operating systems and changes over time, and results can depend on infrastructure configuration and on random initialisation.

Reproducibility is necessary but not sufficient for high-quality research, because reproducing a result can carry through the original author's mistakes, so a critical approach to the methods is needed rather than naively using existing software or statistical methods without understanding them.

Making an analysis reproducible takes time and effort, particularly at the start of a project to agree a testing framework, set up version control and continuous integration, and manage data, and to maintain the pipeline over time.

The upfront time cost of reproducibility is more than repaid later, because a version-controlled reproducible pipeline makes a reviewer's late request for one more analysis fast to run and incorporate and makes the work easy to reuse in future projects.

Being reproducible does not oblige authors to support the expansion and reuse of code and data beyond re-running the exact analyses that produced the published results, so fear of endless user support conflates reproducible with open research.
The primary beneficiaries of well-commented, well-tested code with detailed documentation are usually the research team themselves, and especially the principal investigator and your own future self.

Working reproducibly requires skills not always taught in training programmes, such as data engineering, research software engineering, technical writing for documentation, and project management, which is itself a barrier to reproducibility.

Reproducible research should keep a complete history and provenance of the project, including its data, tools, methods, code, and documentation, which supports research sustainability, fair citation and acknowledgement, and the usefulness of the work.
Reproducible workflows facilitate peer review tremendously by giving reviewers access to the parts of the project needed to validate the research outcomes, review the methods, and test the code.

Lack of reproducibility is one of the major factors leading to paper retractions, and landmark analyses found reproducibility rates of research output of only around 40% in psychology and around 10% in cancer biology.
Publishing work with its underlying data and methods brings fair credit, because such research is cited more often since its outcomes can be broadly replicated and trusted.

Following reproducibility guidelines ensures continuity of your work, letting others or your own future self easily build on the results, reuse the materials, and track and continue the project's progress after a long period.

The terms reproducible and replicable are defined oppositely by Claerbout-Karrenbach and by the ACM, and usage varies by discipline, so a project should state which definition it means to avoid confusion.

Stodden distinguishes computational reproducibility (detail on code, software, hardware, and implementation), empirical reproducibility (detail on non-computational experiments and how data was collected), and statistical reproducibility (detail on statistical tests, model parameters, and thresholds, tied to pre-registration to prevent p-value hacking).

The Turing Way defines a result as reproducible when the same analysis on the same data gives the same answer, replicable when the same analysis on different data gives qualitatively similar answers, robust when the same data under different analysis workflows gives similar answers, and generalisable when replicable and robust findings are combined.

Robust results, obtained by subjecting the same dataset to different analysis workflows such as one pipeline in R and another in Python, show that the work does not depend on the specific programming language chosen for the analysis.
Research can be reproducible without every part being open, because some research uses sensitive data that cannot be shared while still allowing the analysis to be reproducible.
exception: the data is sensitive and cannot be shared openly

statement: The command line is often a beneficial way to interact with a computer, offering efficiency, independence from graphical interfaces, flexibility, and task automation, and some advanced tasks or tools are only available as command-line tools.
Linux and macOS use bash natively, while the Windows command line uses batch script, which is a different language.

A data article is a publication focused on describing a dataset using the traditional journal-article structure, emphasising data collection and methodology rather than interpretation or discussion of results.

Publish a data article to get a dataset peer-reviewed, which archived repository datasets generally are not, increasing the data's visibility, credibility, and usability and giving you credit as a data producer.

The CARE Principles for Indigenous Data Governance (Collective benefit, Authority to control, Responsibility, and Ethics) apply whenever you are collecting data with or that belong to a particular Indigenous community.
When handling data that belongs to an Indigenous or other under-served community, the CARE principles take priority over the benefits of making the data open.
condition: the data belongs to an Indigenous or under-served community

statement: Most data and software licenses do not incorporate Indigenous considerations of data sharing, and Traditional Knowledge (TK) Labels let communities express local conditions for sharing consistent with their existing governance and protocols.
Do not touch the raw data: back it up somewhere reasonable and keep a read-only copy so you can always return to the original information.
Set up a Data Management Plan to decide how the data is managed, which is especially relevant when you collect sensitive data and must plan for consent to share it.
Document everything and keep the documentation together with the data, to ensure the data remains reusable.
Before creating a new schema, storage format, or naming protocol, search for an existing tool or ask colleagues, because something already in use is likely to be better in the long run.
Follow any procedures required by your research group, institute, or country, including ethics, integrity codes, and policies on data management and open science.

Ensure every team member, and an outside researcher in the same field, can find and use the project's data, code, and documentation now and in ten years, supported by regularly maintained documentation and established on- and off-boarding procedures.

Think about your data-collection strategy before collecting data, because unstructured collection can make cleaning take a lot of time, and it is sometimes quicker to restart collection than to fix a messy dataset.
Save an untouched copy of the raw dataset before you begin cleaning, and make all changes in one data file so it does not become a mess to identify the correct latest version.

Validate data by checking that it is complete (no missing or duplicate rows and columns), accurate (valid, unique, consistent IDs, variables, and formatting), and reasonable (no out-of-range or unexpected values), using tables, plots, and summary statistics to surface errors.
Standardise data entries so equivalent values are consistent, for example writing dates uniformly and keeping capitalisation consistent, since a computer treats Yes, yes, and Y as separate responses.
Make each variable hold only one piece of information (tidy data), splitting a variable into multiple variables when more than one thing is measured.

Handle missing data thoughtfully by deciding whether to remove, impute, or mark it as unknown or not applicable, and document that decision transparently, because missing data can itself provide insight into the collection process.
Document your data-cleaning steps in a log that records what you changed, when, and most importantly why, so that others can replicate the cleaning process.

Prevent future data errors at collection time by defining range limits where possible and requiring data entry to avoid unintended blank values, because it is easier not to have to clean data than to clean it.
Treat unexpectedly high or low values carefully during cleaning rather than deleting them blindly, because they could be data-entry errors but may also be the most interesting findings.

Data curation spans capturing, appraising, disposing of, describing, preserving, accessing, reusing, and transforming research data, promoting its use from the point of creation and keeping it accessible in an organised format.
Preserve data by storing it in interoperable or frequently used file formats, which increases the chance that the files can still be opened after several years have passed.
Research data follows a lifecycle of creation, use, publication and sharing, archiving, and reuse or destruction, and the data has a longer lifespan than the research project that creates it.

Research data are the objects used and produced across the research lifecycle, including datasets, code, models, figures, images, and interviews, identified by asking what information backs your conclusions and what others need to understand and replicate your research.
A Data Management Plan is a living document describing how research outputs are generated, stored, used, and shared, acting as a roadmap that helps prevent data loss or breaches and saves time later.

A Data Management Plan should cover six topics: roles and responsibilities, the types and sizes of data and the metadata generated, storage and backup procedures, preservation of outputs after the project, reuse by others including licensing, and costs.
Ensure at least one other person, such as your supervisor or PI, has access to your data, and for personal or commercially sensitive data give access only to individuals who must work with it.
Select a license when you deposit an output on a repository, because it tells others how they can reuse the data, and without a license others cannot reuse it without asking your permission.
Choose a data repository that provides a persistent identifier such as a DOI and has a stated preservation policy specifying how long your outputs will be curated.

When choosing an Electronic Lab Notebook, avoid format lock-in by checking that files export to your preferred formats, and avoid vendor lock-in by having an exit strategy in case the solution is discontinued or you move institutions.

Choosing an Electronic Lab Notebook is a high-stakes, long-term decision because you put your research record and daily workflow into the tool for years, and a poor fit harms productivity and morale while a good fit boosts them.

When choosing an Electronic Lab Notebook, check its backup plans and data-security measures, especially for sensitive data, and prefer a solution with a larger chance of being sustained over the long term.

Electronic Lab Notebook adoption fails when incomplete or inflexible tools add workflow friction, because scientists avoid ill-fitting tools, leading to shadow notebooks, infrequent updates, consistency conflicts over which copy is the source of truth, and information sprawl across disconnected systems.

When picking an Electronic Lab Notebook, benchmark it against a paper notebook, the thing you are actually replacing, rather than only against other ELNs, and identify which paper properties such as physical control and freedom from vendor fees or license terms you need to retain.

Paper notebooks perform an archival function needing little active upkeep and can last decades if kept cool, dry, and dark, whereas electronic data needs much more active upkeep but, if managed properly with backups in multiple locations, can be more resilient to physical threats.

For long-term archiving avoid proprietary formats and prefer open formats, because proprietary formats obfuscate their specification, have a single vendor implementation that is a single point of failure, and may require license activation from a vendor that may no longer exist, so your data's fate is tied to the format you choose.

Scrutinise a tool's data-export quality before adopting it, because being able to export only as PDF may lose a lot of metadata and structure, so evaluate whether you can export your data while retaining its original structure.

Proprietary vendors are incentivised to lock customers in, and data portability that is good during the user-acquisition phase tends to decline once a vendor reaches high market penetration, as when Mendeley began encrypting its local database after being acquired by Elsevier.

For any critical piece of software intended for long-term use, first ask whether there is an open-source solution, whether you could self-host a fully featured instance, whether there is a large active community or institutional backing, and what the data export options and formats are.

With open tools the software development, hosting, administration, and support layers can be separated so you can change any provider independently, unlike a vertically integrated Software-as-a-Service platform, which improves your bargaining position although it may increase procurement complexity.
Even when paying a third party to host an open-source tool, take regular local backups of exports so that you could restore the system with a different host and retain the option to change providers.

An open-source ELN with an open file format does not by itself guarantee you can use your data with other ELN tools without an open ELN standard, and such a standard would reduce the lock-in risk of both open and proprietary tools.

Generic note-taking and personal-knowledge-management apps are often pressed into service as ELNs off-label, and some suit this better than others but may have drawbacks such as a proprietary format with limited export options and no good version history.

The FAIR principles make digital assets Findable, Accessible, Interoperable, and Reusable, all of which support research reproducibility, and the majority of European funders and research institutes now require researchers to make their outputs FAIR.
It is much easier to make data FAIR if you plan to do so from the beginning of the research project, which you can arrange in your Data Management Plan.

For FAIR data, findable requires descriptive metadata and persistent identifiers, accessible requires a known way to obtain the data (possibly with authentication and authorisation), interoperable requires integration with other data and workflows, and reusable requires the data to be well described so it can be used, combined, and extended in different settings.
Making data FAIR is not the same as making it open: accessible only means a procedure is in place to access the data, and data should be as open as possible and as closed as necessary.

The FAIR principles are aspirational, describing a continuum of features and behaviours that move a digital resource closer to FAIRness rather than strictly defining how to achieve it, and they also apply to software.

Find datasets by browsing discipline-specific and multidisciplinary repositories such as Zenodo, OSF, and Figshare, searching data journals and research articles, using your professional network, and using dedicated data-search tools.

Before reusing a found dataset, check its license to confirm you can actually reuse it, remembering that restricted datasets still carry a license and should have a clear application process such as a data request form or contact address.

Before reusing data, evaluate its metadata and documentation for reusability by checking the original research question, how and by whom it was collected, whether the collection methods, instruments, and settings are documented, and whether the information is complete, understandable, and consistent.

Cite any dataset you reuse to credit its creators, in both your research documentation and your published articles, and check how the creators want it cited, since they sometimes prefer you cite an accompanying publication rather than the dataset itself.
Data without metadata is of no use, because metadata provides the provenance and context, such as headings describing what columns and rows contain, needed to understand and use the data effectively.

Write all documentation accompanying data in clear, plain language so users have enough information to understand the source, strengths, weaknesses, and analytical limitations of the data and make informed decisions when using it.

Share a README file with every dataset that describes the methods used for data collection and analysis and the data-specific details such as parameters, variables, column headings, and symbols, so the data can be correctly interpreted and used.

Create a data dictionary or codebook that lists all variables and labels with their numerical value ranges, units of measurement, sources, and classification schemes, aiming that another researcher could analyse and interpret the data using the codebook alone.
Make codebooks human-readable and machine-readable and keep them consistent, so the information can be accessed both by people and by automated approaches.
Store data in logical and hierarchical folder structures with a README file describing the structure, which helps others and your future self find the data.

Use recognised, discipline-specific community metadata standards, which you can identify through resources like FAIRsharing, because standardised metadata is vital for reproducibility and lets heterogeneous data from multiple sources and disciplines be compared and combined.

Document every step of the research process, recording what you did or observed and why, including mistakes and difficulties, specifically enough that someone with a similar background or you in six months could repeat the work with the same results.
Share your methods and protocols openly through a protocol repository such as protocols.io, so that others can reproduce your research.
Personal data is information about living people who can be identified from it directly or indirectly, such as a name, address, or unique identifier.
