Obtain informed, voluntary, and fair consent for any research project involving human participants, and adopt privacy-safeguarding strategies to ensure any sharing or publishing of the data can be done safely.
condition: the research involves human participants

statement: Persistent identifiers are long-lasting references to digital resources that remain valid even if the resource's location changes, and they are fundamental to making research findable, accessible, and citable in the long term.

Ordinary web links suffer link rot, with about one in five reference articles becoming inaccessible within a few years, whereas a persistent identifier uses a resolver that redirects to the resource's current location, so only the resolver's records change when the resource moves.
Assign a persistent identifier such as a DOI to any research output you want others to be able to find, access, and cite.

The scholarly PID ecosystem interconnects: DOIs from DataCite (for datasets, software, and protocols) and Crossref (for articles) identify outputs, ORCID identifies people, ROR identifies organisations, and Funder IDs identify grants, forming a queryable graph of relationships.
Register an ORCID iD to distinguish yourself from every other researcher, collect all your outputs in one place, and keep attribution linked across name changes or institutional moves.

Persistent identifiers support FAIR: they make outputs findable through a unique ID and harvested metadata, accessible by resolving to a landing page that describes access even for restricted data, interoperable through shared resolution infrastructure and standard metadata, and reusable through persistent citation, versioning, and credit.

PID metadata is machine-readable, standardised, cross-domain, and publicly accessible even when the resource itself is restricted, and it complements domain-specific metadata, since PID metadata enables discovery while domain-specific metadata enables reuse.

Provide rich PID metadata, including a description, subject keywords, related identifiers, funding references, contributors with ORCID iDs, and affiliations with ROR IDs, rather than only the required minimum, because rich metadata substantially increases discoverability and the reusability of your outputs.

Deposit research outputs in a trusted repository, which automatically mints the PID and constructs, registers, and exposes the metadata, which is a key advantage over simply hosting files on a personal or institutional website.

Create persistent identifiers throughout the research lifecycle, for Data Management Plans, protocols, raw and processed datasets, computational notebooks, code, preprints, final datasets, and even null results, not only for final outputs.

For most researchers, obtain persistent identifiers through a trusted repository rather than by direct minting, because the repository handles the technical details, provides storage and preservation, and maintains the PID even if you move institutions.
Express DOIs as full URLs beginning with https://doi.org/ in online contexts so they are clickable and resolve through the doi.org resolver to the resource's current landing page.

With repository-based PIDs you do not maintain them yourself, because the repository keeps the PID resolving even if its website is redesigned, keeps the metadata accurate and updatable, and maintains the landing page with current access information.

When a resource must be removed, its PID is not deleted but resolves to a tombstone page explaining why the resource is no longer available, which preserves the scholarly record and the citation network far better than a plain 404 error.
A trusted data repository must earn the trust of the communities it serves and demonstrate that it is reliable and capable of appropriately managing the data it holds.

Long-term archiving repositories differ from platforms like GitHub and GitLab, which are transient collaborative development tools that do not assign persistent identifiers to repositories and have more flexible preservation policies.

Deposit research outputs in a repository to make them FAIR, because it assigns a persistent identifier, describes them with metadata standards, adds a license, provides documentation, and encourages widely-used, sustainable file formats.

Even for data that cannot be made completely open, at least open the metadata and provide an access procedure for credentialed users, so the work stays FAIR because the metadata are findable and there is an access procedure, while remaining secure because you control who has access.

Do not share data only as a paper's supplemental materials, because they get no separate DOI, cannot be updated, are often format-limited, become inaccessible when the article is paywalled with links that break, and hide data that should be a primary research output.

Data available upon request is frequently not actually available, since multiple studies found that only a minority of authors share their data when asked and that recoverability declines steeply over time, so do not rely on request-based sharing for reproducibility.

Submit data to a domain-specific, community-recognised repository where one exists, using a general-purpose repository only when there is no suitable discipline-specific option, because discipline repositories offer more relevant functionality and community standards that make the data more FAIR.

When selecting a repository, check that it is community-recognised and uses your discipline's standards, provides a persistent identifier such as a DOI, offers the access control you need such as restricted access or embargoes, accepts your file formats and sizes, and satisfies any funder, publisher, or institutional requirement.

The choice of repository depends on your discipline, the type of digital output, the file size, the policies and requirements of institutions, funders, and national bodies, and any access restrictions.

Share research data to allow a study to be fully reproduced, to prevent duplicated effort and speed scientific progress, to facilitate collaboration and increase research impact and quality, and to make often publicly-funded research available as a public good.

When sharing data, first decide which data others actually need to reproduce your research, because not all data can be made openly available due to ethical and commercial concerns and some intermediate data may be too large to share.
Share data in a formal, open, and indexed data repository where possible so that it will remain accessible in the long run.

Apply a license to shared data so others know what they can do with it, and make sure your paper and code both link to the data and the data links back to them, to get maximum value from data sharing.

Upload shared data in open, structured, and standardised formats with sufficient documentation and metadata that someone else can understand it, often providing multiple standardised formats so the data can be processed by computers and used by people.

After making your data available, cite the dataset directly in the paper where relevant, include a citation in the reference list, and add a Data Availability Statement at the end of the paper so readers can find the data.

A Software Management Plan is a living document describing how software will be developed, documented, versioned, licensed, archived, and shared during and after a project, supporting traceability, long-term usability, quality assurance, and user support.

Even short one-off scripts written to analyse data are software, and Software Management Plans apply across the research-software spectrum from analysis code to prototype tools to infrastructure software, although the management level differs with the software's purpose and context.

Draft a Software Management Plan during the planning phase of your project alongside your Data Management Plan, determine the software's management level, use an appropriate template, and update it regularly such as when releasing major versions.
Always state the software's purpose in its management plan, because software should be made with a purpose in mind and that purpose determines the level of management it needs.

Inappropriate use of spreadsheets is a major cause of mistakes in the data-analysis workflow, as shown by cases like the loss of COVID-19 data in England and recurring gene-name errors, so spreadsheets should be used with caution.

Treat as data only what can be exported to a text-only CSV or TSV format, and avoid cell formatting, colour, functions, and merged cells, because such presentation-layer modifications are not data and cannot be exported to other software.
Test a spreadsheet's compatibility with reproducible research by exporting it to CSV and reopening it; if you can still get all the information you stored, the data is fine.
Encode highlighting or a categorical flag as an explicit extra data column rather than by colouring cells, so the information becomes part of the data and can be used to filter or sort.

Organise spreadsheet data in tidy format: one column per variable with unique header names, one row per observation, one value per cell, the first row as the header, and header names without special characters or leading numbers.

Enforce consistent values across collaborators using a data dictionary or taxonomy of accepted terms documented in a README, and restrict the accepted values in specific columns where the software allows, since inconsistent entry is a common source of errors.

Define clear rules for missing data points, because NA, NULL, and empty cells can mean different things such as an impossible value, an unrecorded value, or a lost value, and an ambiguous placeholder can be mistaken for a real value; for example use a separate boolean column instead of an ambiguous number.

Ambiguous formats cause data errors: a date like 02-03 means February 3rd in the USA but March 2nd in Europe, and spreadsheet decimal separators differ by locale and program version, so choose unambiguous conventions.

Avoid manually manipulating or analysing data in spreadsheet software, including copy-paste, and instead use scripts or a tool like OpenRefine that automatically records the manipulation steps, because manual steps produce a non-reproducible workflow.

Validate spreadsheet data for consistency, completeness, and correctness before it enters the analysis workflow, checking that numeric columns hold only numbers, names, units, and data types are consistent, empty cells are replaced with a chosen null value, and redundant data is removed.

To store dates reliably in spreadsheets, use separate columns for year, month, and day, because Excel and similar software tend to transform yyyy-mm-dd dates into their own format even when importing from a CSV file.

Record raw measurements such as a length in millimetres rather than a pre-derived category such as longer-than-30cm, so that categorisations can be created automatically later and future analyses are not restricted.

Look for a standard spreadsheet design before making your own, share your design openly once created, keep a version history of the spreadsheet as it evolves, and have the analysis script reference the spreadsheet version number.

When a team collects data in spreadsheets, ensure everyone uses the same software and version and the same template, understands each column and its unit, follows a defined per-column entry standard, designates one person to answer questions, and validates every sheet before it enters the analysis workflow.
condition: multiple people collect data together

statement: Data loss can be catastrophic for a research project and happens often, so prevent it by picking suitable storage solutions and backing up your data frequently.

Portable storage media such as USB sticks are risky and vulnerable to loss and damage, and cloud storage is convenient but you should check its terms of use, ensure compliance with any data-protection rules, and encrypt devices and files when handling personal or sensitive data.

Organise data in a clear, sufficiently nested folder structure (by person, date, project, method, or data type), reusing an existing template, and avoid vague or overlapping folder names and never put personal data in file or folder names.

Use a consistent file-naming convention documented in a README or style guide, and consider starting each file name with its generation date in YYYYMMDD form so files sort chronologically and each gets a unique identifier.

Make file names friendly to both machines and humans: avoid special characters and spaces, use hyphens to separate related chunks and underscores to separate unrelated ones, use lowercase since some operating systems are case-sensitive, zero-pad numbers, keep names short, and avoid personal data.
Be careful when using bulk file-renaming tools, because changes they make can be too rigorous if they are not carefully checked.

Follow good backup practice by keeping two or three copies of your files on at least two different storage media in different locations, ideally automatically, backing up more frequently the more important the data and the more often it changes.

Research Data Management covers how research data is stored, described, and reused, and is a vital part of enabling reproducible research, improving workflow efficiency and the reach and impact of data as it becomes FAIR.

The software dependency stack of even a moderately complex project can be huge, requiring matching versions of packages and tools like pandoc and LaTeX, so capturing a self-contained snapshot of the whole computing environment as a container can be easier than resolving dependencies through a package manager.

A container packages a project with all the parts it needs, such as libraries, dependencies, and system settings, so that anyone can run it as if their machine were identical to the one specified, which makes it easier to transfer projects between very different environments.

Unlike a virtual machine, a container includes only the individual components the project needs rather than a whole virtual operating system, which gives a significant performance boost and reduces the size of the application.

Containers are a more robust way of sharing reproducible research than package-management systems or Binder because they reproduce the entire system used for the research rather than just the explicitly used packages, at the cost of being conceptually harder to grasp and produce.

Images are generated from human-written recipe files such as Dockerfiles, and containers are identical copies instantiated from an image, so to let others reproduce your work you write a recipe, build an image, and share that image for them to run as a container.

Only download and run a container image if it comes from a trusted source, because images can contain malicious code or unknowingly include software with security vulnerabilities, and prefer verified official-image badges.

Specify a version for the base image in a Dockerfile, because although optional it is best practice: it keeps the Dockerfile valid after new releases of the base that might no longer include packages or specific versions you require.
Spend time choosing an appropriate base image, because a suitable one, such as a pre-built image that already includes the R language, can dramatically reduce the work of writing a Dockerfile.

Group related commands into a single RUN block in a Dockerfile to reduce the final image size by avoiding unnecessary layers, and use options like --no-install-recommends and clean the package cache to shrink the image further.

Prefer the COPY command over ADD in a Dockerfile except where ADD's extra capability such as fetching a file from a URL is specifically required, because COPY is more explicit about what is being done.

Data visualisation is an aspect of research data management, because it extracts patterns from data, communicates findings accessibly to a broader audience, and helps identify data-quality issues as outliers and errors become more visible.

Use WORKDIR to change directories in a Dockerfile rather than RUN cd, because after each RUN statement the image is saved and following commands restart at the root level, so a RUN cd has no lasting effect and leads to errors.

Use CMD in a Dockerfile for commands that should run as soon as the container opens, as opposed to RUN which runs during setup, so users do not have to run those steps themselves or even know they are needed.

Exclude large, unneeded files from the Docker build context by listing them in a .dockerignore file, because everything in the Dockerfile's directory and below is sent to the daemon and unnecessary files make building the image slow.
Every container opened from an image starts completely fresh, so work done inside a container is lost when it closes unless a volume is used to store that work and load it into future containers.

To persist work across container sessions, mount a volume with a descriptive name and a target directory, since only work within that target directory is saved into the volume and reloaded when you reopen the project.

Adding a user to the docker group grants high-level host access with a trivial privilege-escalation route, because the Docker daemon runs as root by default and a bind mount can expose the entire host filesystem to the container with root permissions.

Rootless containers, run by a normal user without sudo or the root account, never have more privileges than the account that runs them, which is a strong security advantage over running containers as root or through the Docker daemon.

Podman is a free, open-source, daemonless container engine with a Docker-compatible command-line interface that unprivileged users can run and that works with Open Container Initiative and Docker images, avoiding the Docker daemon's implicit privilege-escalation risk.

Singularity was created for high-performance computing and reproducible research and does not require root access to run containers, unlike historic Docker, letting users bring their software and dependencies to a shared HPC system without administrators installing or maintaining them.

Singularity can build container images from Docker images and can natively use host GPUs from Nvidia (CUDA) or AMD (ROCm) without root privileges, and its single-file image format is convenient for copying work to a cluster.

When passing host GPUs into a container, ensure the application inside the container is compatible with the host's driver stack, for example matching CUDA versions, because a mismatch is likely to cause problems.
condition: the container uses host GPU passthrough

statement: A container recipe file is not reproducible in itself, because the build process depends on online sources that may be updated so the same recipe can produce different images, so true reproducibility requires storing the actual built container images.

Store actual container images, not just recipes, in a citable long-term archive such as Zenodo, which mints a DOI and is geared toward long-term storage and discoverability, rather than relying only on Docker Hub.

Point any software installed in a Singularity container to a global, user-independent configuration file, because Singularity binds $HOME by default and the current user's settings can silently override the image-specific configuration, which is dangerous for reproducible research.

Ways of capturing a computational environment split into those that capture only the software and its versions (package management systems) and those that replicate the entire environment including the operating system and settings (virtual machines and containers), and the best choice depends on the project.

A package management system installs and tracks the software and versions used in an environment and can export a file specifying those packages and versions, which others use to replicate the environment.

Use separate, easily interchangeable environments, for example with Conda, so that each project pins its own package versions and you avoid the poor choices of freezing versions, risking one project by upgrading for another, or manually reinstalling packages when switching projects.

Conda can capture and export a computational environment and recreate it from a configuration file, and it works without admin privileges, which is useful on high-performance computing facilities because it creates new environments rather than changing the machine's overall system environment.
Create a new Conda environment for every project you start rather than working in the base environment.
Pin the versions of packages and of the language in a Conda environment, for example python=3.7.1 and scipy=1.2.1, so the environment is reproducible.

Prefer installing packages with conda install, which provides a Conda-tailored build, and use pip only when no Conda version exists; when mixing them install as many requirements as possible with Conda before using pip, because running Conda after pip can overwrite or break pip-installed packages and produce a hard-to-reproduce state.
Export a Conda environment to a human-readable YAML file and recreate it from that file, so that researchers can quickly reproduce one another's computational environments.

An exported environment file lists more than the explicitly installed packages and can include OS-specific dependency packages, so it may require some editing to be portable to different operating systems.

A virtual machine packages a whole computer as an app running on a host and acts as a quarantined area, so tools downloaded or settings changed inside it only affect the VM and keep the reproducer's own research safe, and a broken VM can simply be deleted and remade.

Virtual machines can be exported as a single file and imported by another researcher to open a working copy of the project with all the software, files, and settings in place, without the pain of setting it up themselves.

Prefer defining virtual machines declaratively in plain text, such as a Vagrantfile, over distributing full VM images, because the text can be checked into version control, is small and fast to share, reproducibly builds the environment, and can target multiple hypervisors.
Maintain a project's development environment definition, such as a Vagrantfile, alongside the source code so every contributor can use the same environment with minimal barriers.
YAML is an indentation-based markup language that is easy to read and write and is widely used for configuration files, including for defining computational environments and GitHub Actions workflows.
Quote YAML string values that contain any special characters such as square brackets, braces, colon, greater-than, or pipe, because leaving them unquoted causes parse failures.
Use spaces, not tabs, for indentation in YAML, because tabs can produce many subtle parsing errors even when the resulting YAML looks valid.
Do not load a YAML file or generate a computational environment from any file you did not write unless you trust its source, because it is possible to include malicious code in such files.

Every computer has a unique computational environment of operating system, installed software, package versions, hardware, and configurations, so an analysis moved to a different computer has no guarantee of running or producing the same results unless that environment is captured.
To make research reproducible, capture the computational environment in which it was conducted in a way that lets others replicate it.
Semantic versioning defines each software version with three numbers in the pattern MAJOR.MINOR.PATCH, incremented respectively for significant changes, added functionality, and bug fixes.

A perfectly valid piece of code can give different results depending on its computational environment, for example dividing 1 by 5 prints 0.2 in Python 3 but 0 in Python 2 because Python 2 applies integer division, which is why the environment must be captured.

Uncaptured computational environments affect three parties: researchers who cannot confidently return to a project after software changes, collaborators who face a minefield of multi-environment bugs some of which stay undetected, and science because publications are disconnected from the underlying analysis and environment.

For research to be reproducible, publish and distribute the entire contained analysis, the whole software stack from data files up through the library stack, so it is mobile and can reliably be executed on other systems, not just its results.

Before requesting a code review, ensure the new code meets the project's standards, has documentation and tests matching those standards, that the new tests pass locally, and that the rest of the codebase's tests still pass.

A reviewer should check the code against the project's required standards and style guide, that tests and documentation conform, that the code is understandable and correct with no bugs, that security issues are handled correctly, and that legal and licensing requirements are met.

At the program level, review whether the program is split into clearly separated modules that are as small as possible with a clear hierarchical or layered dependency structure, and whether the design can be simplified.

For a security review, compartmentalise input and output into dedicated modules, validate untrusted data in the input module and pass only validated data to other parts, and minimise where untrusted data is present.
condition: the software is accessible to the outside world

statement: For a legal review, document the licenses of all modules and libraries used, ensure their requirements are met by including license and copyright statements where needed, and confirm the licenses are compatible with each other and with the project license.

At the file or change level, check that each function documents its intent, inputs and outputs with units, and pre- and postconditions, performs its intended function correctly, is easy to understand, is free of redundant or duplicate code, has loops that terminate correctly, and has debugging or logging code removed.
When reviewing the security of new code, check the errors returned by any library you use, validate all data inputs, check and properly encode output values, and handle invalid parameters correctly.

Code review is an effective method for improving software quality: McConnell reports unit testing finds about 25% of defects, function testing 35%, integration testing 45%, and code review 55 to 60%, so no method is sufficient alone and they should be combined.

Because a robust test suite should catch straightforward bugs before review, code review's real value is as a second line of defence and in highlighting inadequate tests, checking documentation fitness, ensuring readability, enforcing style, and building group knowledge and cohesion.
When you are tagged as a reviewer, first check whether you have enough knowledge about the new changes to do a good job in a reasonable amount of time.
Avoid letting the same reviewer-coder pairs persist over long development cycles, because it can lead to the same kind of groupthink that the review process is designed to avoid.
In code reviews, always assume good faith on both sides and be constructive, because review necessarily involves criticism, potentially between two complete strangers.

Keep code reviews as objective as possible by deciding subjective coding preferences at the project level in advance and pointing to those documented preferences, rather than passing an opinion off as fact.

Differentiate crucial from optional review comments, using phrasing like You must for non-optional changes and You might for suggestions, so coders know what is essential and inexperienced coders are guided without being over-nitpicked.

Review code in small chunks incrementally, reviewing no more than about 400 lines at a time and preferably under 200, no more than about 500 lines per hour, and no more than an hour at a stretch, because beyond these limits the defect-finding success rate drops quickly.

All review of code is valuable, including informal or ad-hoc over-the-shoulder peer review, which can form a key preliminary component even in a highly formalised review pipeline and save stress once the formal stage begins.

Make many small review comments attached to specific lines rather than one big block of text, and file many small pull requests rather than one large one, so that different issues stay separate and the review does not become unwieldy.
Make completion and sign-off of a review a formal precondition of performing the merge, and adopt this principle even for small or informal projects.

Use a risk assessment based on a piece of software's complexity and the impact of a mishap to choose which sustainability practices it needs, because using none leaves it exposed while using all of them from the outset can get in the way of innovation, so find the right balance for now and revisit it when circumstances change.

Every piece of software has different needs to be sustainable, and those needs can change over time, as when a throwaway shell script gradually evolves into a large multi-university workflow control system.

Measure software complexity broadly through line count, number of dependencies and functions, number of use cases, and range of platforms, and measure impact by what happens when the software fails, from a few minutes of annoyance to a retracted paper or lives lost, taking a broad view of how the software is used.

Acceptance testing determines whether software satisfies all of the requirements from the business or user's perspective and is one of the last tests before delivery, though it may be unnecessary for research software written by the researcher who will use it.
exception: the software is research software written and used by the same researcher

statement: Regression testing retests after changes by comparing the outputs to those recorded before the change and raising an error if they differ, ensuring that enhancements or defect fixes have not adversely affected functionality not directly associated with the change.

Automate regression testing, because it is next to impossible to do satisfactorily by hand given how tedious it is, and it is surprisingly easy to break your own code without noticing even when working alone.
Regression tests detect only that a piece of code's output has changed, not that it is correct; testing correctness is the remit of other kinds of tests.

Adopt test-driven development by writing unit tests before the code, so the tests describe a contract the code must comply with, which ensures the code is correct as written and forces it to be broken into small, modular, testable units.

Test-driven development checks whether the thing has been done correctly, while behaviour-driven development checks whether the correct thing has been done, focusing on user needs, which is worth considering when research software is written with a large user base in mind.

Test stochastic code either by fixing a random-number seed to make it reliably reproducible or by running it many times and testing the distribution of results within a tolerance, being aware that seed-based tests are brittle to changes in how many random numbers are consumed and distribution tests are slow and can occasionally fail even when the code is correct.
condition: the code has a random or stochastic element

statement: For outputs that are judged by whether they look right, automate basic sanity checks such as a value being within a set percentage of the previous time step or having no negative values, rather than relying on time-consuming human eyeballing, accepting that such checks cannot catch every error but suffice for most cases.

Compare non-integer floating-point numbers for equality only within a given tolerance rather than exactly, because floating-point numbers are approximations (0.1 plus 0.2 is not exactly 0.3) and results can depend on the compiler, processor, and architecture, and most testing frameworks provide an approximate-equality function for this.
Write some tests, any tests, because testing one tiny thing in a code of thousands of lines is infinitely better than testing nothing, so do something even if you cannot test everything.

Run the tests regularly, ideally automated at intervals or through continuous integration, because a test suite that is rarely run is useless and long gaps between runs make failures hard to diagnose and make it unclear which interim results are still valid.

Weight your test suite toward many fast tests such as unit tests and few slow tests such as system tests, running the lightweight tests frequently and the long tests once per day overnight, scaling the number of each kind to how long it takes to run.

Document how to run the tests, including any required test datasets, configuration adjustments, and software such as testing frameworks, ideally with scripts to set up the needed resources, for your future self and anyone reproducing your work.
Make the cases you test as realistic as possible, so that if your real data is messy with many null values, your test dataset should be too.
Use a testing framework to make writing and running tests easier, choosing one for your language, learning its features, and making use of them.

Aim for high code coverage, the proportion of code run by your tests, but beware the illusion of good coverage: coverage can be high while the code produces the broadly right answer for the wrong reasons, so favour tests that isolate small chunks of logic and test the same code in multiple ways.

Use test doubles such as dummy objects, fakes, stubs, and mocks to eliminate external dependencies from a test, so that when a test fails the source of the failure traces clearly to the code under test rather than to a dependency like the network or a real database.

Integration testing combines individual units and tests them as a group to expose faults in their interaction, because units can each pass their own tests yet fail to integrate, as when one unit outputs data in one order or unit that another expects differently, or the Mars Climate Orbiter crash caused by one component using feet and another metres.

Unit-test each unit and fix any bugs before starting integration testing, because a bug in an individual unit will almost certainly make the integration tests fail even when the integration itself is correct.

When integration testing top-down or bottom-up, use test stubs to simulate the outputs or inputs of the sections not currently under test, so that upper-level tests do not break due to bugs in lower-level units.

Integration testing approaches differ: Big Bang combines all units at once, Top Down tests high-level sections first, Bottom Up tests low-level sections first, and Sandwich or Hybrid combines the two; choose the approach that best suits the structure of your project.

Tests are either positive, checking that something works, or negative, checking that something raises an error when it should, such as flagging particles faster than light; both kinds can exist at any test level and a thorough suite contains tests at all levels.

Embed runtime tests as checks within the program, such as verifying a computed population is non-negative or that a function's inputs and outputs are the expected size, to catch logic errors and edge cases early and minimise the blast radius, reporting detected problems via exceptions.

Smoke tests are very quick initial checks of basic functionality and environmental assumptions run at the start of each testing cycle, and a failed smoke test causes rejection of the build and stops further testing until the problem is resolved.

System or end-to-end testing tests the complete integrated software's outward functionality against the specified requirements and can also test properties beyond correctness such as performance, migration to another environment, stress and scale, usability, and recovery.

Run slow system or end-to-end tests only after the lower-level smoke, unit, and integration tests have passed, and because they cannot cover every route through a program, prioritise the most common, most important, and most breakage-prone paths, running them automatically each night.

A unit is the smallest testable part of software, typically a function or method, and unit testing validates each unit in isolation, replacing any external dependencies with stub or mock implementations to focus the test entirely on the code in question.

Unit tests give researchers confidence when changing and maintaining code and make development faster, because testing small pieces of code pinpoints the cause of a bug far more quickly than large-scale tests or no tests, and catches bugs early while their impact is still limited to small units.

Unit testing strongly incentivises writing modular code, broken into small functions that each accomplish a simple task, which is easier to test and much easier to reuse than one long non-modular script.

Write unit tests that are independent of each other, so that if unit A uses a result from unit B you test A with a test double rather than really calling B, otherwise a failure could be due to a fault in either A or B and the bug is harder to trace.
Aim to cover all paths through a unit, paying particular attention to loop conditions, and in addition to behaviour cases write cases that check the code's performance.

When you find a defect in your code, write a test that exposes it before fixing it, because you will then catch the defect if it is not fixed properly, your test suite becomes more comprehensive, and you are unlikely to write the test once the defect is already fixed.

Researcher-written code forms part of a huge portion of research, so mistakes in it can make results partly or entirely unreliable, which is why testing code thoroughly and frequently is vital to ensure reliable, reproducible research.

It is very easy to make coding mistakes that have catastrophic research consequences, as when a single wrong sign led to five paper retractions and a feet-versus-metres mismatch between two pieces of software lost a Mars satellite, which is why tests are vital.

Write tests because you are short on time, not skip them because you are, since tests are the time-saving and safe option compared with repeatedly checking a huge program by hand or redoing months of contaminated work.

Formalise the ad-hoc print-statement checks you write while coding into functions kept as an independently and automatically runnable test suite, because the extra labour is minimal but it gives far greater confidence the software is correct and increases the likelihood defects are found.

Testing makes research more reproducible by answering how we even know the code works, and if tests are deleted rather than saved the proof cannot easily be reproduced, captured in the slogan better software, better research.
Make each commit one simple change, commit no generated files, and write meaningful commit messages with a summary of about 50 characters in the present-tense imperative.
Develop each new feature on its own informatively named branch, keep the main branch clean, and merge other people's changes into your work frequently.
When dealing with a merge conflict, make sure you fully understand both versions before trying to resolve them.

Research data is only rarely invariant, being extended, renamed, reorganised, updated, or corrected over a project, so if the data underlying a result changes without version control, reproducibility is threatened and the original results may not be reproducible.

Version-control data and other large files in a similar way to code and manuscripts to ensure reproducibility and capture provenance, meaning the precise subset and version of data a set of results originates from.

Git works best with small text files and struggles with large or binary files, because hosts cap file sizes such as GitHub's 100MB limit, large versioned files slow cloning and fetching, and a large file added by accident is tedious to purge, so plan ahead and avoid big repositories.
Use specialised tools that integrate with Git, such as Git LFS, git-annex, DataLad, DVC, or submodules, to version-control and share large or binary data while keeping the Git repository small.
condition: the project contains large or binary files

statement: Data-versioning tools add access complexity, since a newcomer can see a large file exists but cannot download or view it without cloning the repository and running git-annex or DataLad commands, so weigh this accessibility trade-off and consider disabling such tools for critical binary files like presentations or PDFs.

Use branches to keep working code safe by developing a new feature on a branch so you do not risk breaking the main working code, and if a feature branch does not work out you can simply delete or abandon it rather than unpicking your changes.

Keep the main branch containing only work that is complete, tested, and rightfully belongs there, keep each branch to a single feature by only making changes related to that feature, and give branches sensible descriptive names.

Always write a commit message that explains what you did, why you did it, and what is impacted, describing what the code is doing rather than the code itself, for example Change number of simulations run by the program to 10 rather than Change N_sim to 10.

Make commits atomic, each doing one simple thing completely such as adding a function or renaming a variable, because committing many unrelated changes together makes errors hard to troubleshoot and undoing the commit may throw away valid useful work.

Stage the specific files to be committed by name rather than adding everything with git add ., to avoid unintentionally bundling unrelated changes together, while recognising that a single atomic unit of work may still legitimately span multiple files.

Do not commit files that are regenerated from other committed files unless they take hours to regenerate, because generated files clutter the repository and can carry features like timestamps that cause file conflicts; instead list them, and environment-specific configuration files, in a .gitignore file.
exception: the generated output would take hours to regenerate

statement: A Git and GitHub workflow benefits research projects by backing up data through pushing, letting you work across computers, tracking contributions, and providing project-management tools, but GitHub alone is not enough because data versioning, folder structure, and legal or jurisdictional concerns need extra care.
Prefer a Git platform provided as open infrastructure, such as a university GitLab or a self-hosted lightweight open-source platform, over a proprietary one.
Keep your main branch always stable and only merge into it work that is finished and tested, for example developed and validated on a separate branch.

A merge conflict occurs when incompatible changes are made to the same file on different branches, and Git marks the conflicting sections with conflict markers so you can manually edit the file to merge them and then commit the resolved version.
Before resolving a merge conflict, fully understand the changes and how they are incompatible to avoid making things more tangled, remembering that your previous versions remain safe.

The best way to deal with merge conflicts is to avoid them in the first place by keeping branches clean and focused on a single issue, involving as few files as possible, and keeping the lines of communication open with everyone working on the branches.

Commits serve as checkpoints that let you safely save, revert, switch between, and compare versions of individual files or the whole project, without cluttering the directory with manually numbered copies like version_1 and version_2.

A local repository is linked to a web-hosted clone, usually called origin, and pushing shares your changes online so others can obtain their own clone, make changes, and submit a pull request for you to integrate.

A pull request lets a contributor who cannot directly edit a repository, because they are not an owner or admin, propose getting the changes from their branch or fork integrated into the project's main branch.

When contributing to another project, keep your fork in sync with the upstream repository and get all upstream changes into your local main before you create a branch or make a pull request, because an out-of-sync copy leads to conflicting file contents when merging.
Avoid the git rebase command, because it rewrites history and can be troublesome if not communicated with others working on the same branch, and instead use pull or fetch followed by merge.
git pull combines git fetch and git merge, whereas using git fetch on its own stores the fetched commits as a remote branch so you can review the changes before merging them.

Version-control data of any size and attach the data in precise versions to the code and manuscript, so that when the underlying data changes you can update the repositories and recompute your scripts to assess whether the results are replicable while capturing which data a given figure was created from.

Publishing the data, the code and results, and the manuscript as separate but linked version-controlled repositories lets a reader backtrace every step taken to create a result back to the original data, and can bundle data, code, and software environments together for others to reproduce the work.

Easy-to-use, well-documented tools help scientists do better and more reproducible science, especially because many scientists receive no formal training in version control or research data management.

Version control is a systematic approach to recording changes made to a file or set of files over time, so that you and your collaborators can track the history, see what changed, and recall specific versions later when needed.

Manual versioning by naming files v01 and v02 and tracking changes in an external document is impractical when many files change, as when writing code or working with data, so version control software is highly recommended in those cases.

Add a clear, concise comment to each version snapshot, because it makes it easy to get a fast overview of the changes in each version and to find what you are looking for when you need to go back to a past version.

Reproducibility requires providing both the code and the data used to produce a figure, and because data and analysis code evolve over time, version control is needed to record what was changed when in order to provide provenance information.

Version control provides provenance of which version of code and data produced a figure, a version history explaining what changes each version contains, hides older versions so the working directory stays uncluttered while they remain accessible, and lets changes made by different people be tracked and often automatically combined.

Advanced version control systems such as Git, Mercurial, and SVN provide powerful tools including accessing the version history and keeping control over the main version, beyond what real-time collaborative tools like Google Docs or Dropbox offer.
Version control can be applied to nearly any type of file, not just code, and because data can be volatile, versioning it improves the reproducibility of scientific analyses.

Version control makes research more transparent and easier to reproduce and build upon because all your actions are recorded, and hosting services like GitHub and GitLab add structured ways to communicate and collaborate through pull requests, code reviews, and issues.

condition: When a completed project's materials are needed for authorized follow-on research or institutional use.
exception: Disclosure remains limited by applicable secrecy and confidentiality duties.

statement: Academic evaluations should use adequate comparative data or search evidence, analyze scientific, technical, and economic dimensions honestly, provide detailed feedback, and avoid promotional superlatives unsupported by prescribed validation.
condition: When reviewing projects, results, awards, transfers, or public claims about research status.

statement: A reviewer must disclose relevant interests and follow the review body's recusal decision, avoid private contact and compromising gifts, keep materials and deliberations confidential, and never reuse an applicant's unpublished ideas or plans.
condition: When conducting peer review or formal academic evaluation.

statement: Scholarly criticism should follow close reading and substantive analysis, remain centered on the work and evidence, represent facts proportionately, and avoid personal attacks, appeals to status, or retaliation.
condition: When criticizing an academic argument, method, or result.

statement: Research involving people or identifiable private information requires prior assessment and approval by the appropriate institutional and authorized bodies, qualified operators, and responsible faculty supervision of participating students.
condition: Before beginning human-subject research or privacy-sensitive investigation.

statement: Human-subject research must minimize avoidable risk, obtain informed consent from the participant or legal representative, avoid coercion, deception, and improper inducement, protect privacy, and preserve the right to withdraw.
condition: For research involving human participants.
exception: Limited disclosure may be methodologically necessary in some medical or psychological designs, but requires specific ethical justification and oversight.

statement: A literature review should be grounded in broad reading of original, representative, reliable, and current sources; synthesize rather than list them; distinguish the reviewer's analysis from source content; and preserve source meaning.
condition: When authoring a scholarly review.

statement: A compilation or authored compilation must organize prior material under an original framework, cite borrowed passages and complete references as appropriate, and obtain permission before reproducing another person's work as a chapter; a nominal bibliography cannot substitute for attribution.
condition: When producing a compilation, textbook, handbook, or authored compilation from existing works.
exception: A pure compilation may place complete references by chapter or at the end when its genre does not require every source to be marked in the body, but reproduction rights still apply.

statement: Plagiarism includes unattributed copying of ideas, data, methods, formulas, code, or expression even after abridgment, reordering, synonym substitution, restructuring, mosaicing, or added commentary, and it also includes reusing one's own published wording without citation.
condition: When borrowed substantive content is presented publicly as the author's own.
exception: A genuinely independent creation is not plagiarism merely because it resembles another work.

statement: Fabrication includes inventing samples, methods, experiments, observations, results, publications, patents, achievements, credentials, or other research records that do not exist.
condition: When nonexistent material or activity is represented as real in research or professional records.

statement: Falsification includes manipulating materials, equipment, procedures, source records, or data selection so that the research record no longer reflects what actually occurred and instead supports a desired conclusion.
condition: When a real research process or record is altered or selectively represented.
exception: Transparent, justified transformations or exclusions that preserve an auditable account are not falsification.

statement: Research integrity depends on truthful experimental procedures and durable original records; loss or deletion of source data makes verification harder and weakens the credibility of everyone and everything connected to the work.
condition: When research results depend on empirical procedures and recorded data.

statement: Suspected experimental fabrication or falsification may require specialist investigation and reconstruction or repetition of the experimental process because manipulated conditions and data can be difficult to detect directly.
condition: When inconsistencies, failed replication, or insider evidence raise a credible concern about empirical records.

statement: Duplicate submission occurs when the same authors submit the same paper or a substantively similar version to multiple venues simultaneously, or submit it again after knowing it has been accepted or published, without informing the editors.
condition: When venue exclusivity applies by law, agreement, or editorial practice.
exception: A later submission made after a valid rejection or release from exclusivity is not covered by this definition.

statement: Redundant publication occurs when manuscripts substantially repeat hypotheses, methods, samples, data, figures, arguments, or conclusions but fail to cross-reference and disclose their relationship.
condition: When an author republishes the author's own prior work or closely overlapping work.
exception: Republishing another person's work is plagiarism rather than self-redundant publication.

statement: Splitting one study into overlapping papers, changing only the title, rearranging sections, combining the same content differently, changing format, or translating the paper does not by itself create a distinct publication.
condition: When the papers retain the same principal information or substantive content.
exception: A genuinely distinct research question and contribution, transparently linked to related reports, may justify a separate paper.

statement: A complete paper may follow an oral presentation, abstract, poster, or preliminary report if the earlier disclosure is identified and was not a formally published full paper.
condition: When converting preliminary dissemination into a full research report.
exception: A full paper in formally published conference proceedings is not merely preliminary dissemination.

statement: Permissible secondary publication requires full disclosure of all similar earlier reports, cross-citation, submission of relevant prior material, and any written consent required from the first and later editors.
condition: When seeking to republish a consensus document, meeting record, internal report, international edition, translated major finding, or substantially expanded study.
exception: If either venue's rules or rights holder prohibit republication, disclosure alone does not authorize it.

statement: When an undisclosed duplicate publication is discovered, the responsible authors should notify the editors, withdraw the duplicate, and apologize; an unaware coauthor should still report the problem and seek withdrawal after learning of it.
condition: After duplicate submission or publication has occurred.

statement: A university bears direct responsibility for investigating alleged misconduct by its institutions and members and should maintain an authoritative academic investigation body with an operational office and workable procedures.
condition: When misconduct is alleged within the university's jurisdiction.
exception: Matters reserved to courts, regulators, publishers, or funders may also require referral or coordinated jurisdiction.

statement: Misconduct investigations must establish facts and evidence through objective, fair, lawful, and standardized procedures while protecting complainants, preserving respondents' dignity and lawful rights, and clearing people or organizations subjected to unfounded accusations.
condition: During institutional investigation and adjudication of alleged academic misconduct.

statement: Consequences for substantiated misconduct should be proportionate to its nature and severity and may include employment discipline, project suspension, fund recovery, loss of awards or eligibility, scoped disclosure of findings, and referral of suspected legal violations.
condition: After a fair process substantiates academic misconduct.
exception: The available sanction must be authorized by applicable law and institutional or sponsor rules.

statement: Academic integrity, research norms, and relevant intellectual-property rules should be required elements of induction for new teachers and of undergraduate and graduate education, with integrity conduct included in staff and leadership assessment.
condition: When universities design training and performance systems.

statement: Research assessment should prioritize substantive quality indicators such as new problems, materials, data, viewpoints, methods, and theories rather than raw output counts, and should use discipline-specific standards, peer review, and representative works.
condition: When institutions evaluate researchers, projects, theses, publications, or awards.

statement: Evaluation systems should include conflict recusal, collective decision procedures, reviewer-accountability records, publication of appropriate results, and feedback mechanisms.
condition: When designing formal academic review and personnel-evaluation processes.
exception: Confidential information should remain protected when results or reasons are disclosed.

statement: Research governance should expose application information appropriately, recheck contested materials, publish decisions when appropriate, and maintain a complaint channel so that project and result evaluations remain transparent and contestable.
condition: When operating project review, result certification, or related oversight.
exception: Disclosure must respect legitimate privacy, confidentiality, and legal restrictions.

statement: Institutions should distinguish research misconduct from genuine scholarly disagreement, encourage innovation, and tolerate good-faith failure while still investigating evidence of deception or serious norm violations.
condition: When triaging a complaint or judging an unsuccessful or controversial research result.
exception: Innovation or failure is not a defense for fabrication, falsification, plagiarism, or other intentional deception.

statement: Academic publishers and journals should act as integrity gatekeepers by enforcing research norms and developing review practices, including reciprocal author-reviewer anonymity where appropriate, that reduce plagiarism and low-quality redundant publication.
condition: When designing editorial screening and peer-review systems.
exception: The guide presents reciprocal anonymity as a model to explore rather than a universally mandatory design.

statement: Universities and education authorities should establish accountable integrity leadership, coordinate responsible units, audit their own performance regularly, and maintain durable prevention, investigation, education, reward, and sanction mechanisms.
condition: When building an institution-wide academic-integrity program.
